Q: A neural network and backpropagation you can inspect
explain:
The capstone maps a two-component input x to four hidden activations h and one output logit z. W1 has 4×2 weights, b1 has four values, W2 has four weights and b2 has one value: 8+4+4+1=17 trainable parameters. For hidden unit j, h_j=tanh(W1_j dot x+b1_j). The output logit is z=sum_j W2_j h_j+b2, and p=sigmoid(z)=1/(1+exp(-z)). Nonlinearity matters: composing linear maps without activations still produces a linear map.

For target y in {0,1}, binary cross-entropy can be computed stably from the logit as max(z,0)-z y+log(1+exp(-abs(z))). This avoids taking log(0) after a saturated sigmoid. Its derivative with respect to z is p-y. Therefore dL/dW2_j=(p-y)h_j, dL/db2=p-y, and the hidden pre-activation derivative is (p-y)W2_j(1-h_j^2). Multiplying that by each input component gives the two W1 gradients for hidden unit j. Average each gradient across the batch before updating.

An autograd engine records operations and applies equivalent local chain rules in reverse. In PyTorch, tensors carry shapes and optional gradient tracking; a training step typically clears old gradients, computes predictions and loss, calls backward, then steps an optimizer. Gradients accumulate unless cleared deliberately. Evaluation mode and disabled gradient recording are different controls: modules such as dropout change behavior with train/eval mode, while no_grad reduces graph recording. Neither automatically moves tensors between CPU and GPU.

The standard-library implementation exposes the math so you can inspect and finite-difference every parameter. Larger production models should use tested tensor libraries, proper initialization, batch handling, accelerator-aware kernels and reproducibility controls. Loss falling is necessary evidence here, but the independent gradient check is what catches many superficially plausible backward-pass errors.
example: A tiny network fits its training rows but the held-out loss increases. Verify loss/gradient shapes and a numerical derivative check. Compare train and validation curves under fixed data splits. Evaluate regularization, early stopping or simpler baselines without tuning on the final test. Result: A correct backpropagation implementation can still overfit.
takeaway: If training steps use gradients from a previous batch, inspect accumulation and zeroing. If gradients vanish, inspect activation saturation, scale and the chain of multiplications.

Q: Compare convolution, recurrence and attention before selecting an architecture
explain:
A dense layer applies a learned affine map to its input representation. Convolution reuses a local kernel across spatial or temporal positions, sharing parameters and expressing a locality assumption. With three input channels, sixteen output channels and a three-by-three kernel, an ordinary convolution with one bias per output channel has 16×3×3×3 + 16 = 448 parameters. Output shape still depends on stride, padding and input size; parameter count is not an estimate of activation memory or latency.

A recurrent model updates a hidden state from the next input and its previous state. Unrolling that recurrence exposes a sequence of dependent computations for backpropagation. Hidden-state ownership matters across batches: carrying state between unrelated examples can leak information, while detaching state changes the backward path. Gated recurrent variants change how information is retained, but they still need a declared sequence and masking contract.

Attention combines value representations through weights computed from queries and keys. A causal language model restricts which token positions may influence each prediction, while an encoder can use a different context policy. Position representations, tokenization and masks are part of the model’s semantics. A larger attention model is not automatically a better choice for a small image or latency-constrained task; compare a suitable convolutional or other baseline under the same evaluation design.

Whatever the architecture, distinguish the forward loss, its gradients and the optimizer step. Set training/evaluation mode deliberately, and separately choose whether to retain a backward graph. Dropout or running normalization behavior can change without changing the weights. Measure actual task quality and hardware behavior, then inspect a minimal failure such as an unexpected tensor axis, a stale hidden state or a future-token leak. The linked autograd and causal-adapter programs provide runnable checks for those boundaries, while the small parameter calculation is only a shape/count illustration.
example: Calculate 448 convolution parameters by hand, then change the number of input channels. Explain why a larger image changes activation work without changing the kernel parameter count. For a sequence model, separately specify whether state is reset or carried between examples.
takeaway: An architectural inductive bias, a tensor shape, a measured memory peak and a generalization result are different pieces of evidence.

Q: From scalar derivatives to NumPy and PyTorch
explain:
The scalar network exposes every derivative. The NumPy/PyTorch bridge computes the same function with batched arrays, so its first obligation is agreement, not a faster training curve. NumPy builds an 8-by-2 feature matrix and an eight-element target array using float64 values. torch.from_numpy shares CPU storage with that array; a later NumPy mutation can therefore affect the tensor. Copy deliberately when ownership requires isolation.

A 17-element leaf tensor holds exactly the scalar implementation’s parameters. Slicing and reshaping form W1=(4,2), b1=(4,), W2=(4,) and b2=scalar. With features X=(8,2), X@W1.T+b1 produces eight rows and four hidden values. tanh preserves the shape; multiplying by W2 returns one logit per row. Binary cross-entropy with logits computes the same mean objective as the stable scalar formula.

Before training, the bridge compares the loss and every autograd derivative against the independently written scalar implementation. It also runs torch.autograd.gradcheck, which uses numerical perturbations. These are separate checks: a shared wrong objective can pass an implementation comparison, while a correct gradient of the wrong task still does not solve the intended problem. Preserve explicit targets and held-out evaluation.

The training loop clears gradients, computes the current objective, calls backward and steps SGD. Omitting zero_grad accumulates previous gradients and changes the optimization algorithm. Evaluation is wrapped in no_grad because no backward pass is needed. This functional fixture has no dropout or batch normalization; if such modules are added, model.eval changes their mode separately from gradient recording. The script uses one CPU thread, a fixed initial parameter sequence and small synthetic splits. Its result is a reproducibility check under the tested package versions, not a performance or generalization claim.
example: Manual derivatives and autograd disagree by a large factor for the same batch. Fix inputs, parameter values, dtype and loss reduction. Compare every parameter gradient before an optimizer update. Check mean versus sum reduction, broadcasting and detached computation paths. Result: A controlled cross-implementation comparison localizes the mismatch before long training runs.
takeaway: A mismatch often comes from batch averaging, transposed weights, dtype, gradient accumulation or a changed activation derivative. Inspect shapes before adjusting tolerances.

explain:
A token is not necessarily a word or character. Byte-level vocabularies can represent any UTF-8 input, while learned merges combine common byte sequences into larger units. The attention lab implements one illustrative byte-pair merge and verifies exact roundtrips for accented text and an emoji. It does not train BPE or reproduce a production tokenizer. Real tokenizer assets, normalization, special tokens and chat formatting must match the selected model; changing them can change both cost and behavior.

For one attention head, Q has shape (number of queries, d), K has shape (number of keys, d), and V has shape (number of keys, value width). QK-transpose produces a score for every query/key pair. Dividing by sqrt(d) moderates score scale; row-wise softmax turns each query’s scores into weights. Multiplying those weights by V returns one weighted value vector per query. The weights’ row sums are one; their interpretation still depends on the learned projections and masking.

In the one-dimensional worked case, q=1, keys=[1,0], values=[2,4]. Scores are [1,0], weights are approximately [0.731059,0.268941], and output is 0.731059×2+0.268941×4=2.537883. Subtracting the maximum score before exponentiation leaves softmax unchanged and avoids overflow. The browser exercise includes a very large-logit fixture to make this numerical boundary observable.

Causal attention masks future positions so training and autoregressive generation obey the intended dependency order. Position information is supplied through an architecture-specific mechanism, such as positional embeddings or rotary transformations; attention alone does not encode arbitrary token order. Multi-head attention repeats learned projections and combines their outputs. Residual paths, normalization and feed-forward sublayers complete a transformer block; a diagram of only Q/K/V is not a full transformer.
example: A two-position attention row has logits [1,0] and values [2,4]. Subtract the maximum logit before exponentiation. Softmax weights are approximately [0.731059,0.268941]. The weighted value is 0.731059×2+0.268941×4=2.537883. Result: The output follows a normalized weighted combination, with dimensions and numerical stability visible.
takeaway: Shape errors often swap key length and feature width. Softmax over the wrong axis can produce valid-looking numbers with the wrong meaning.

Q: Training objectives, decoding and cached inference
explain:
A decoder language model is commonly pretrained to predict the next token from its prefix. The training objective compares model predictions with known next tokens; generation instead repeatedly chooses a token, appends it, and evaluates the next step. Teacher-forced training can process many positions together under a causal mask. Decoding choices such as greedy selection, temperature scaling and top-p sampling change which sequence is produced, not the learned weights.

Greedy decoding picks the largest score at each step and can still produce an incorrect answer. Temperature scales logits before probabilities are sampled; it does not provide a calibrated factual confidence score. Top-p chooses a probability-mass nucleus according to the implementation’s exact ordering and boundary rules. A fixed seed helps repeat sampling under a fixed environment, but changing kernels, batching or library versions can still affect results. Define which reproducibility guarantee an evaluation requires.

During autoregressive decoding, previous tokens’ keys and values can be reused rather than recomputed from scratch. The attention lab checks prefix K/V reuse against equivalent full-prefix attention for a small fixed single-layer case. In a real transformer, every relevant layer and head has cached tensors, so cache memory grows with batch size and context length as well as head dimensions and storage precision. Prefill and decode have different compute and bandwidth profiles.

The context window is a computational limit, not evidence that every included fact will be used correctly. Context packing needs relevance, ordering, provenance and sufficient space for output. Multimodal systems introduce modality-specific encoders or token representations, alignment and additional privacy considerations; more modalities do not remove the need for grounded evaluation. Benchmark a representative workload across latency, memory, accuracy and unsafe failure cases rather than treating a context-length number as overall quality.
example: An autoregressive decoder has already computed a prefix and generates one more token. Retain compatible prefix key/value tensors under the same model and positional convention. Compute the new token’s query/key/value work. Attend over cached prefix plus the new position without treating another user’s cache as interchangeable. Result: KV reuse avoids recomputing compatible prefix K/V work but consumes growing memory.
takeaway: If incremental output differs from full-prefix computation, inspect masking, cache positions, model mode and projection reuse before assuming numerical noise.

Q: Quantization, LoRA, distillation and model evaluation
explain:
For a simple symmetric int8 quantizer, choose scale=max(abs(weight))/127, round each weight divided by scale to an integer, and reconstruct by multiplying by scale. For values within the represented range, nearest rounding introduces at most roughly half a scale unit of absolute error, subject to floating-point details. The lab verifies this bound on a fixture. The all-zero case needs an explicit scale convention. Real quantization can use per-channel scales, different zero points, calibration and specialized kernels; lower bit width alone does not prove faster inference.

If a weight matrix W has output width m and input width n, a low-rank update can be written delta_W=B A, where A has shape (r,n) and B has shape (m,r). The update uses r(n+m) parameters rather than mn when r is small. Apply the update as B(Ax), with any declared scaling, and keep the base weights fixed according to the chosen method. LoRA still needs representative training data, optimizer state, compatible target modules and evaluation; a small adapter is not automatically a small total serving footprint.

Fine-tuning changes model parameters or adapters; retrieval changes the supplied evidence; prompting changes the input instruction. Choose the cheapest method that solves the measured failure and respects data requirements. Distillation can reduce serving cost, but a student may inherit teacher errors or lose rare capabilities. Evaluate it against independent labels and safety constraints rather than only agreement with its teacher.

Keep model and tokenizer versions, decoding configuration, dataset provenance and metric definitions with the report. Measure quality slices, false refusals, unsupported claims, privacy leakage, robustness and latency/cost. The tiny training capstone’s perfect synthetic accuracy is a reproducible implementation check, not a deployment benchmark. A release decision requires a representative held-out dataset and a documented threshold for both acceptable outcomes and unacceptable side effects.
example: A smaller numerical representation reduces model weight storage but measured latency gets worse. Confirm the quantization format, kernels and hardware actually used. Measure end-to-end latency, memory and quality on the same tasks. Compare with a nonquantized baseline and inspect conversion overhead. Result: Memory reduction does not imply a universal inference speedup.
takeaway: An adapter loaded into the wrong model revision can silently invalidate results. A quantized model that is smaller but slower may be using unsuitable kernels or suffering from transfer overhead.
